figures.caption: Lienzo de Tlaxcala, Cortes introducing Christianity; 1773 copy of a Tlaxcalan pictorial from the 1550s.

books.section: Topic 1.6 Cultural Interactions Between Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans
The Early Colonial Era: Spain Colonizes the New World

primary_sources: Lienzo de Tlaxcala, c. 1550s (1773 copy), public domain

options.text: It proves that Cortes himself drew the first Lienzo.
options.misconception: Cortes was a soldier, not a Tlaxcalan artist; the copy proves nothing about him as a painter.

options.text: A copy is always more reliable than the original it copies.
options.misconception: A copy can preserve an original, but it is not more reliable than the original itself.

options.text: It preserves a Native view of the encounter.
It shows that Tlaxcalan art never changed over two centuries.
options.misconception: One copy tells us nothing about how Tlaxcalan art changed; that claim needs other evidence.

rationales.general:
1. Ask what Spanish texts give. The Spanish side of the encounter.
2. Ask what this image gives. The Tlaxcalan side: Native artists picturing the arrival of Christianity.
3. Ask whether a copy keeps that value. A faithful copy still carries the Native view forward.
4. Rule out the rest. Copies are not more reliable than originals, Cortes did not draw it, and one copy cannot show centuries of change.
Remember: a source is valuable for the view only it gives, even when it reaches us as a copy.
rationales.C: Spanish texts give the Spanish side of the encounter. This drawing gives the Tlaxcalan side: Native artists picturing the arrival of Christianity. A later copy still carries that Native view forward.
rationales.A: Nothing ties Cortes to the drawing. He was a soldier leading the conquest, not a Tlaxcalan artist.
rationales.B: Copies are useful, but they are never more reliable than the originals they copy. The copy's value is what it preserves, not a greater reliability.
rationales.D: A single copy cannot show two centuries of change. That claim would need many works from many dates.

stem: This image is a 1773 copy of a Tlaxcalan pictorial from the 1550s. Why is it still valuable evidence about cultural interaction in the 1500s?

stimulus.source_note: Lienzo de Tlaxcala, Hernan Cortes introducing Christianity; 1773 copy by Manuel de Yllanez of a Tlaxcalan pictorial from the 1550s; public domain, Wikimedia Commons.
stimulus.text: This drawing is a 1773 copy of a Tlaxcalan pictorial from the 1550s, the Lienzo de Tlaxcala. At the center stands a tall cross marked INRI, with a ladder and the instruments of the Passion. Two armed Spanish soldiers stand beside the cross. On each side, Tlaxcalan men in feathered headdresses gesture toward the cross.
